topics.title: [DIS] CKB IDL: Interface Description Language and Discoverability for CKB Scripts

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] CKB IDL: Interface Description Language and Discoverability for CKB Scripts
recent_posts.author: OWK50GA
recent_posts.content_text:
Summary
One-paragraph Overview:
This proposal requests a grant of $5,000 to build the next phase of the CKB IDL lifecycle: an open-source, testnet-first Script Registry for publishing, discovering, and independently verifying CKB script interfaces, together with IDL 0.1.1 empty-interface support, Molecule interoperability, and TypeScript support. It builds on the already released IDL 0.1.0 specification, Rust derive/export tooling, Rust client, binding CLI, and reference lock scripts.
Deliverables include:
Release CKB IDL 0.1.1, adding explicitly empty witness interfaces, with corresponding schema, specification, conformance vectors, canonicalization, commitment, and documentation updates.
Extend the released Rust toolchain and client to generate, bind, verify, encode, and decode explicitly empty witness interfaces alongside structured interfaces.
Integrate the existing Rust client and CLI with Registry publication and testnet verification workflows for wallet and transaction-builder consumption.
Build the open-source CKB script Registry backend for immutable package releases, IDL and artifact storage, publisher authentication, metadata, and public APIs
Implement testnet deployment and verification and automated discovery, connecting registered artifacts to live CKB code cells, while distinguishing cryptographically bound, legacy-attested, and unverified interfaces.
Build the public registry user interface for search, script/interface inspection, verification status, IDL viewing, integration guidance, and transaction-builder snippets
Add Molecule-to-IDL support to allow existing Molecule-based CKB scripts to generate and publish compatible IDL interfaces without abandoning Molecule
Update TypeScript support for CKB IDL 0.1.1, to enable TypeScript script interface consumers
Grant Amount Requested: $5,000 USD equivalent, paid in CKB at the USD value at the time of disbursement
ETA to completion: 15 weeks from Initial Funding
CKB Wallet or Funding Address: ckb1qzda0cr08m85hc8jlnfp3zer7xulejywt49kt2rr0vthywaa50xwsq2yyt9j8q6rvv06t3cnjdjvtu64t93ccqgyw9h55
Project Introduction
CKB scripts are powerful and flexible, but their interfaces are often difficult for wallets, transaction builders, indexers, and other developers to discover and use safely, without prior knowledge of the script author, source repository, or serialization implementation. A script may expect a particular lock-witness format, optional fields, nested data, tagged variants, or an encoding convention that is only documented in its source code - or not documented at all. This creates friction for integration: a developer must already know the script, find its repository, understand its serialization rules, and manually reproduce its transaction-building logic.
Consider a time-locked inheritance-vault application. Its frontend currently hard-codes the lock and Type Script deployment hashes and CellDeps, owns a Molecule codec for vault cell data, and implements bespoke create and claim transaction flows. A wallet or another frontend cannot infer this from the script’s code hash; it must find the source code and reproduce integration-specific knowledge. A bound IDL gives the ecosystem a verifiable interface artifact to discover, inspect, and - where the relevant profile is supported - decode or encode without reverse-engineering raw bytes.
The idea is partly inspired by Bitcoin’s Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (PSBT) workflow, which makes transaction data portable between independent tools. CKB’s programmable scripts introduce an additional requirement: transaction data alone cannot explain what an unfamiliar script expects. CKB IDL is intended to provide that complementary interface layer, allowing tools to discover and verify script-specific requirements before constructing or signing a transaction.
CKB IDL addresses this gap by providing a standard, machine-readable description of a script interface. An IDL document describes the witness data a lock script expects, including its fields, types, semantic labels, and encoding. The document can be canonically serialized, hashed, and bound to the deployed executable through an append-only trailer in the code cell. This means an integration tool can retrieve an interface document from a registry, independently verify that it matches the deployed script, and use it to construct or validate the script’s witness data.
The project is not only an IDL format. It is an end-to-end lifecycle:
Script authors derive or export an IDL from their Rust types or Molecule schemas.
Tooling validates, canonicalizes, and binds the IDL to a deployable executable.
A client library verifies the binding and exposes a structured witness object to wallets and transaction builders.
A public CKB Script Registry makes scripts, deployment information, source references, and optional interface artifacts discoverable, allowing both IDL-enabled and existing scripts to participate.
The Registry is designed as a discovery and evidence layer, not a new source of trust. The authoritative integrity check remains the binding between the canonical IDL hash and the deployed code-cell data. Registry records will distinguish between cryptographically bound interfaces, manually attested legacy interfaces, and unverified submissions, so downstream tools can make informed trust decisions.
Why now?
The foundational pieces are now sufficiently mature to connect into a usable system. The project already has a Rust derive/export workflow, an IDL 0.1.0 specification, a Rust client capable of verification and witness-object handling, binding tooling, and practical lock-script examples. The next step is to turn these separate capabilities into a public workflow that CKB developers can actually discover, publish, verify, and consume.
Molecule compatibility is a priority because Molecule is already widely used for CKB serialization. The project will define an initial Molecule encoding profile and generator that parses supported .mol schemas, preserves their existing wire format, and emits self-contained, canonical CKB IDL documents. Authors will be able to add wallet-facing descriptions and semantic labels through lightweight schema comments, with an optional metadata overlay where necessary. This gives existing Molecule-based scripts a practical path into Registry discovery and client integration without requiring them to abandon Molecule or migrate their encoded data.
By establishing this lifecycle early—before script interfaces become fragmented across incompatible conventions—CKB can gain a shared interface layer that is language-neutral, verifiable, friendly to wallet builders, and open for ecosystem adoption.
Team & Roles
Name/Handle: Wilfrid / @OWK50GA
Role: Solo developer covering protocol design, backend, and frontend, and design
Experience/Relevant background: I am a fullstack software developer with experience building on Blockchain. I am a Bitcoin enthusiast and Chaincode Labs BOSS challenge alumnus. While learning CKB, I studied the implications of its Cell Model and identified the lack of a standard, discoverable, machine-readable interface layer for scripts.
Current Status
The project has progressed beyond the idea stage. The core of the CKB IDL lifecycle has been designed and prototyped across several open-source repositories.
Completed or substantially implemented work includes:
IDL 0.1.0 specification: a dedicated specification repository defining the document structure, linear encoding profile, canonical JSON requirements, commitment model, error categories, conformance vectors, and compatibility guidance.
Rust derive and export tooling: ckb-idl-derive provides Rust macros for describing witness interfaces, including primitive types, fixed byte arrays, vectors, optional fields, nested structures, and explicitly tagged unions. A host-side exporter supports complete nested IDL generation.
Rust client library: ckb-idl-client can parse IDL documents, verify canonical commitments against a deployed executable’s binding trailer, validate witness bytes, and expose decoded witness data as structured objects.
Binding CLI: ckb-idl-cli provides commands for validating IDLs, generating and inspecting bindings, packaging artifacts, and verifying bound executables.
Reference lock scripts: multiple example lock scripts demonstrate optional fields, nested structures, tagged authorization choices, typed vectors, threshold/multisignature-style data, and commitment-based deployment artifacts.
Initial TypeScript work: an earlier TypeScript implementation exists and provides a starting point for the IDL 0.1.0 upgrade.
Community discussion: the initial interface-language proposal was published on Nervos Talk and introduced the derive, validate, and commitment direction to the ecosystem.
The work is now at the transition point from protocol/tooling prototypes to ecosystem infrastructure. The remaining work is to stabilize the released workflow, add Molecule compatibility, complete TypeScript support, and build the public registry through which scripts and their interfaces can be published, discovered, independently verified, and integrated.
Relevant links:
Initial proposal and community discussion: LS-IDL: a Lock Script Interface Description Language for CKB
Rust derive/export tooling: ckb-idl-derive
IDL specification: ckb-idl-spec
Rust client: ckb-idl-client
Binding CLI: ckb-idl-cli
Reference lock scripts: ckb_sudt_script
Architecture & Design
The proposed system completes the CKB IDL lifecycle: script authors describe an interface, bind it to a deployable executable, publish it for discovery, and allow wallets or transaction builders to verify and consume it.
The full System Design Document is available here: CKB IDL System Design Document. It covers the data model, trust model, storage, deployment operations, security controls, and open design decisions in greater detail.
IDL 0.1.1 will add explicit support for empty witness interfaces. A script that requires no structured witness_args.lock payload still benefits from a discoverable identity, deployment record, verification status, documentation, and a machine-readable declaration that its lock-witness interface is intentionally empty.
Authoring and binding
Script authors define their witness interfaces through one of three paths:
Rust derives and exporter: Rust scripts use ckb-idl-derive to describe supported witness types and generate an IDL document.
Molecule-to-IDL generation: Molecule schemas are converted into compatible IDL documents, allowing existing Molecule-based scripts to join the same discovery and client workflow.
Manual legacy-IDL authoring: existing scripts without an embedded commitment can still publish a manually attested interface document.
The ckb-idl-cli validates the resulting IDL, canonicalizes it according to the IDL specification, calculates its SHA-256 digest, and appends a compact binding trailer to the compiled executable. The bound executable is then deployed as CKB code-cell data.
The trailer commits the deployed executable to the exact canonical IDL document. This gives a consumer a way to verify that an interface retrieved from the Registry actually corresponds to the deployed script.
Script Registry
The CKB Script Registry is an open-source, testnet-first discovery and evidence service for CKB scripts, independent of their implementation language, serialization format, or adoption of CKB IDL.
Scripts can be registered with or without an IDL document. Each registry entry can contain script identity, deployment references, publisher information, release metadata, source references, documentation, and optional interface artifacts.
CKB IDL is the first deeply supported interface standard, enabling cryptographically verifiable interface discovery and structured witness integration. Scripts without IDL remain discoverable, although they do not receive IDL-specific verification or encoding capabilities.
Scope and Focus
Although the Registry is designed as general-purpose infrastructure for CKB scripts, the primary focus of this proposal is completing the CKB IDL lifecycle. The Registry will accommodate scripts without IDL artifacts from its first release, ensuring that its architecture does not depend on adoption of a particular interface standard. However, the development effort, verification tooling, client integrations, and reference workflows funded by this grant will prioritize CKB IDL publication, discovery, verification, and consumption. Broader script-related capabilities can be developed incrementally without requiring a redesign of the Registry.
The initial registry architecture consists of:
a Rust API service for public reads, publisher authentication, package publication, validation, and release metadata
a background worker for CKB RPC verification, confirmation checks, code-cell liveness checks, retries, and candidate discovery
PostgreSQL for publishers, namespaces, releases, deployments, verification claims, jobs, and audit events;
content-addressed object storage for immutable IDL documents, manifests, and artifacts;
a TypeScript web frontend for search, package pages, interface inspection, deployment evidence, and integration guidance.
GitHub OAuth is sufficient for initial publisher authentication. CKB wallet ownership proofs will be added later, but are not necessary to establish the first useful publication workflow.
The registry is not a general-purpose transaction explorer. It focuses on script interfaces, artifacts, deployment evidence, and integration information, not generic chain analytics.
Consumer Verification
Wallets, SDKs, frontends, and transaction builders use the Registry for script discovery and integration information, but do not need to trust its claims blindly.
A consumer flow is:
Resolve a script or package through the Registry.
Retrieve its registered metadata, available artifacts, and deployment references.
Independently verify the relevant deployment claims against CKB, including the referenced code cell and executable identity.
Inspect the available interface artifacts, if any.
For scripts with a cryptographically bound CKB IDL:
Retrieve the canonical IDL document and the deployed executable’s code-cell data.
Read and validate the executable’s binding trailer.
Canonicalize the retrieved IDL and calculate its SHA-256 digest.
Confirm that the digest matches the commitment in the binding trailer.
Use the verified interface to decode existing witness data or encode structured witness inputs for transaction construction.
For scripts with manually attested CKB IDLs:
Retrieve the published IDL and its associated publisher attestation.
Validate the IDL document against the specification and inspect its declared relationship to the script.
Use the interface for encoding, decoding, or integration where appropriate, while recognizing that its correspondence to the executable has not been cryptographically established.
For scripts without CKB IDL:
Access the available deployment information, source references, documentation, and integration guidance.
Integrate using the script’s existing conventions or supported tooling.
These workflows distinguish verification of on-chain deployment facts from verification of interface commitments. A script may have independently verified deployment information without having a cryptographically bound IDL.
The Registry provides discovery and evidence rather than serving as a trusted authority. For bound interfaces, consumers can independently verify the IDL-to-executable relationship. For manually attested interfaces, the Registry identifies the source and limitations of the attestation without presenting it as equivalent to cryptographic binding.
Verification States
The registry records independent claims rather than presenting every listing as “verified”. A package may be:
Cryptographically bound: the canonical IDL digest matches the binding trailer in a deployed executable.
Manually attested: an identified publisher has documented an existing script without a trailer binding.
Unverified: submitted or discovered, but not yet sufficiently validated
Historical, spent, deprecated, or withdrawn: retained for transparency, but not presented as an active recommended deployment.
This allows existing scripts to be documented now without representing them as equivalent to newly bound IDL-enabled scripts.
Design rationale
The design is deliberately lightweight for the first release. It avoids arbitrary source builds, uploaded-code execution, on-chain Registry contracts, package dependency resolution, and a general explorer infrastructure. The Registry validates artifacts and chain facts; it does not execute scripts or claim to audit them.
This keeps the MVP focused on the core value proposition:
author → generate → validate → bind → deploy → publish → discover → verify → consume
It also provides a practical adoption path for both new Rust-based scripts and existing Molecule-based CKB development. The architecture is testnet-first, open-source, and designed to grow into mainnet support only after the publication, verification, resource-limit, and operational workflows have been demonstrated in practice.
Practical Use Cases, Ecosystem Integrations & Key Benefits for CKB
CKB IDL would provide a common interface layer for CKB scripts: one that makes script requirements understandable to both humans and software without weakening CKB’s flexibility or requiring a centralized authority to be trusted.
1. CCC: Generic Transaction Construction for Custom Scripts
CCC provides TypeScript transaction construction and wallet integration for CKB applications. Integrating an unfamiliar custom script still requires developers to understand its deployment, witness encoding, and transaction requirements.
CKB IDL would let CCC-based applications discover and verify published script interfaces, generate structured witness inputs, and encode witness data before passing transactions to CCC for signing and submission. This reduces script-specific integration work without replacing CCC’s existing responsibilities.
2. CellScript: Cross-Language Script Interoperability
CellScript already provides compiler-level interfaces, generated builders, and a registry for its development ecosystem. CKB IDL would complement these capabilities by providing a language-neutral interface artifact for deployed scripts.
CellScript-generated scripts could publish standard IDLs that Rust applications, TypeScript frontends, wallets, and other consumers can independently verify and use without understanding CellScript-specific compiler metadata.
3. Type Scripts: Programmable Game-State Transitions (Future)
A CKB game could represent player positions and game state using cells governed by Type Scripts. A future Type Script IDL profile could describe state-cell data, required move inputs, and structural transaction requirements, enabling frontends to construct transactions while the Type Script enforces valid state transitions.
This use case is outside the proposed IDL 0.1.1 scope but illustrates the value of extending CKB IDL beyond lock-witness interfaces.
4. A verifiable public registry
The Script Registry will provide a public place to search scripts, inspect interfaces, view deployment evidence, and find integration guidance. Importantly, it will not ask wallets to trust a registry database blindly. The registry is a discovery and evidence layer; the client can independently verify the IDL commitment embedded in the executable’s code-cell data.
This distinction is important for CKB: public convenience does not need to compromise self-verification.
Even when a script has no CKB IDL, developers can discover its registered identity, deployment locations, source references, and available documentation through the same Registry.
5. Support for existing as well as new scripts
Not every existing CKB script can be rebuilt with an IDL commitment. The Registry will support manually authored legacy IDLs, but label them distinctly from cryptographically bound interfaces. This allows the ecosystem to document important existing scripts immediately while preserving an honest trust model.

Out-of-Scope / Possible Future Funding Needs
This proposal is deliberately focused on a testnet-first, open-source implementation of the CKB IDL lifecycle and Script Registry. The following are not included in the requested $5,000 budget and may require later community discussion, follow-up grants, or independent funding.
Mainnet Registry launch and production SLA: Mainnet support will be considered only after testnet verification, backup recovery, monitoring, rate-limit testing, and client integration have been demonstrated.
Formal third-party security audit: The Registry does not execute uploaded code and this proposal does not deploy a new on-chain Registry contract. However, formal audits may be appropriate before a mainnet launch or if future on-chain components are introduced.
Long-term maintenance and infrastructure costs: The proposal covers development and initial testnet operation, not indefinite hosting, monitoring, support, or maintenance.
CKB wallet ownership proofs: MVP publisher authentication uses GitHub OAuth. Linking a publisher identity to CKB address ownership is a future enhancement.
Reproducible source-build verification: The Registry may link source code, but independently rebuilding source and proving it produces the registered executable requires controlled build infrastructure and is not included.
Type Script interface support: The initial IDL profile focuses on lock-witness interfaces. Type Script support requires separate design work, particularly around script arguments and hash_type = type resolution.
On-chain Registry contract, governance, or tokenomics: The first Registry is an off-chain discovery and evidence service. No Registry token, governance mechanism, or on-chain publication contract is proposed.
Full OpenZeppelin-style curated library or template marketplace: The Registry may later support recommendations and reusable templates, but the MVP focuses on verifiable artifact publication and discovery.
Full package dependency resolution: Package dependencies, version solving, and cross-package compatibility analysis are not required for the initial Registry.
Universal language and encoding support: Molecule integration and TypeScript support are included. Broader language bindings and support for other possible encoding systems are future work.
Multi-region high-availability infrastructure: The MVP does not include Kubernetes, multi-region active-active deployment, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Redis, or comparable operational complexity.
Risk & Mitigation
Risk
Impact
Mitigation
Registry scope becomes too broad
Delays delivery or produces an incomplete product
The project is limited to testnet, a focused publication/verification workflow, a basic public frontend, Molecule support for the supported profile, and TypeScript compatibility. Mainnet, audits, and marketplace features are explicitly deferred.
CKB deployment verification is more complex than expected
May delay reliable verification of deployments or liveness.
The Registry begins with reference scripts and a narrow binding-trailer verification path. Chain checks run in retryable background jobs and record explicit pending or failed states.
RPC outages, stale results, or reorganizations
Deployment state may be temporarily uncertain.
Store block evidence, use configurable confirmation thresholds, recheck liveness, use retries with backoff, and treat RPC failure as pending verification rather than failure.
Molecule mapping has unsupported constructs
Some Molecule schemas may not map losslessly to IDL 0.1.0.
Begin with a documented supported subset, publish clear errors for unsupported constructs, and validate against real schemas rather than promising universal coverage.
Low early Registry adoption
Fewer publishers and interfaces at launch.
Publish reference scripts, support manual legacy-IDL attestation, provide clear integration examples, and make the Registry useful even before broad ecosystem participation.
Misleading or malicious publisher metadata
Users could mistake a listing for an audit or endorsement.
Separate cryptographic binding, publisher identity, source availability, audit, and recommendation claims. Avoid a single generic “verified” badge
Resource-exhaustion or storage abuse
Could increase cost or affect availability.
Enforce upload, decompression, document-size, nesting-depth, queue, rate, and per-publisher limits. Use immutable blobs and cacheable public reads.
Solo-developer execution risk
Delivery speed depends on one maintainer.
Work is divided into independently demonstrable milestones, builds on already released tooling, uses open repositories, and keeps major future features out of scope.
CKB price volatility
The CKB-denominated amount may fluctuate.
The grant is requested as a USD equivalent, with each CKB disbursement calculated at the USD value at the time of payment.
Closing / Call to Action
CKB already enables developers to build highly flexible scripts. The missing layer is a shared, verifiable way for those scripts to describe their interfaces and for other developers to discover and safely integrate them, without needing to have pre-existing knowledge of the source code of the scripts.
The IDL 0.1.0 toolchain provides the foundation. This proposal funds the next step: a practical testnet lifecycle where interfaces can be generated from Rust or Molecule, bound to executables, published through an open Registry, independently verified by clients, and consumed by wallets and transaction builders.
The goal is not to create another centralized source of truth. It is to make CKB scripts easier to discover and reuse while preserving the ability of clients to verify the interface-to-executable relationship directly from CKB code-cell data.
Feedback on the Registry data model, Molecule integration, TypeScript workflow, verification policy, and testnet rollout is welcome. We appreciate the community’s consideration and look forward to building this openly with the CKB ecosystem.

Glossary
Term
Meaning
Artifact
An immutable published file or byte sequence, such as an IDL document, manifest, executable, or source archive.
Binding Trailer 1
The append-only metadata trailer, placed at the end of bound executable code-cell data. It contains the committed canonical IDL digest and metadata needed to parse it.
Bound executable
A compiled script executable with a valid IDL binding trailer appended to its bytes.
Canonical IDL bytes
Converting an IDL JSON document into one deterministic byte representation before hashing.
Canonicalization
Converting an IDL JSON document into one deterministic byte representation before hashing.
CKB code cell
A CKB cell whose data contains a script executable that can be referenced by a lock or type script.
Code hash
The CKB hash used to identify executable code-cell data for script resolution.
Code-cell data hash
A hash of the complete data stored in a specific code cell, including an IDL binding trailer where present.
Consumer
A wallet, SDK, transaction builder, frontend, or other application that retrieves and uses an IDL.
Cryptographically bound
An interface status indicating that the SHA-256 digest of canonical IDL bytes matches the digest stored in the deployed executable’s binding trailer.
Deployment
A concrete on-chain location for an artifact, identified by network, transaction hash, and output index.
Deployment inclusion
Evidence that a declared transaction output exists in an observed confirmed CKB block.
Deployment liveness
The currently observed state of whether a code cell remains unspent and available on-chain.
Digest
A fixed-length cryptographic hash output. IDL 0.1.0 uses SHA-256 for the canonical IDL commitment.
Encoding profile
The rules used to serialize and deserialize fields in an IDL interface, such as the initial CKB IDL linear encoding profile.
Field path
A stable path describing where a validation or decoding error occurred within an IDL document or witness object.
GitHub OAuth
The initial publisher-authentication method used by the Registry. It verifies control of a GitHub account, not ownership of a CKB address.
Hash type
The CKB script field that determines how code_hash should be interpreted, such as data or type.
IDL
Interface Description Language: a machine-readable document describing a CKB script interface, its fields, types, encoding, and optional semantic labels.
IDL digest
The SHA-256 hash of canonical IDL bytes. This is the value committed in Binding Trailer 1.
Legacy IDL
A manually authored IDL for a script that does not contain an embedded binding trailer.
Manually attested
An interface status indicating that a publisher supplied an IDL for a script but no cryptographic executable binding has been verified.
Manifest
An immutable metadata document describing a publication bundle and its artifact digests.
Molecule
A serialization framework widely used in the CKB ecosystem. The proposed Molecule integration generates compatible IDL documents from supported schemas.
Namespace
A publisher-controlled naming scope used in package coordinates, such as publisher-name/package-name.
Object storage
Blob storage used for immutable files such as IDLs, manifests, and optionally executables.
Outpoint
A CKB reference to a specific transaction output, consisting of a transaction hash and output index.
Package
A human-readable Registry project identity that may contain multiple immutable releases.
Publisher
An authenticated account or organization that submits and manages Registry packages and releases.
Registry
The off-chain discovery, publication, storage, and verification-evidence service for CKB script, their deployments, metadata, and optional interface artifacts.
Release
An immutable versioned publication under a package coordinate, such as namespace/package@1.0.0.
Reorganization (reorg)
A chain event in which previously observed blocks are replaced, requiring deployment evidence and confirmation status to be rechecked.
Semantic type
An optional label that gives a structural field a wallet-facing meaning, such as an address, signature, public key, or amount.
Structural type / wire type
The actual encoded representation of a field, such as u64, bytes, a fixed byte array, vector, struct, or union.
Testnet-first
The rollout policy in which the first public Registry and verification workflow target CKB testnet before any mainnet deployment.
Transaction builder
Software that assembles CKB transactions, including script arguments, witnesses, inputs, outputs, and signing data.
TypeScript client
The planned frontend-oriented IDL library used to retrieve, verify, encode, and decode IDL interfaces in TypeScript applications.
Unverified
A Registry state where an artifact or interface has been submitted or discovered but does not yet meet a defined verification status.
Witness object
The structured in-memory representation of decoded witness fields that a client can validate, display, or encode into witness_args.lock.
Witness interface
The IDL description of data expected in a script witness; IDL 0.1.0 initially focuses on witness_args.lock.

Project Introduction

CKB scripts are powerful and flexible, but their interfaces are often difficult for wallets, transaction builders, indexers, and other developers to discover and use safely, without prior knowledge of the script author, source repository, or serialization implementation. A script may expect a particular lock-witness format, optional fields, nested data, tagged variants, or an encoding convention that is only documented in its source code - or not documented at all. This creates friction for integration: a developer must already know the script, find its repository, understand its serialization rules, and manually reproduce its transaction-building logic.

Consider a time-locked inheritance-vault application. Its frontend currently hard-codes the lock and Type Script deployment hashes and CellDeps, owns a Molecule codec for vault cell data, and implements bespoke create and claim transaction flows. A wallet or another frontend cannot infer this from the script’s code hash; it must find the source code and reproduce integration-specific knowledge. A bound IDL gives the ecosystem a verifiable interface artifact to discover, inspect, and - where the relevant profile is supported - decode or encode without reverse-engineering raw bytes.

The idea is partly inspired by Bitcoin’s Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (PSBT) workflow, which makes transaction data portable between independent tools. CKB’s programmable scripts introduce an additional requirement: transaction data alone cannot explain what an unfamiliar script expects. CKB IDL is intended to provide that complementary interface layer, allowing tools to discover and verify script-specific requirements before constructing or signing a transaction.

CKB IDL addresses this gap by providing a standard, machine-readable description of a script interface. An IDL document describes the witness data a lock script expects, including its fields, types, semantic labels, and encoding. The document can be canonically serialized, hashed, and bound to the deployed executable through an append-only trailer in the code cell. This means an integration tool can retrieve an interface document from a registry, independently verify that it matches the deployed script, and use it to construct or validate the script’s witness data.

The project is not only an IDL format. It is an end-to-end lifecycle:

  • Script authors derive or export an IDL from their Rust types or Molecule schemas.

  • Tooling validates, canonicalizes, and binds the IDL to a deployable executable.

  • A client library verifies the binding and exposes a structured witness object to wallets and transaction builders.

  • A public CKB Script Registry makes scripts, deployment information, source references, and optional interface artifacts discoverable, allowing both IDL-enabled and existing scripts to participate.

The Registry is designed as a discovery and evidence layer, not a new source of trust. The authoritative integrity check remains the binding between the canonical IDL hash and the deployed code-cell data. Registry records will distinguish between cryptographically bound interfaces, manually attested legacy interfaces, and unverified submissions, so downstream tools can make informed trust decisions.

Why now?

The foundational pieces are now sufficiently mature to connect into a usable system. The project already has a Rust derive/export workflow, an IDL 0.1.0 specification, a Rust client capable of verification and witness-object handling, binding tooling, and practical lock-script examples. The next step is to turn these separate capabilities into a public workflow that CKB developers can actually discover, publish, verify, and consume.

Molecule compatibility is a priority because Molecule is already widely used for CKB serialization. The project will define an initial Molecule encoding profile and generator that parses supported .mol schemas, preserves their existing wire format, and emits self-contained, canonical CKB IDL documents. Authors will be able to add wallet-facing descriptions and semantic labels through lightweight schema comments, with an optional metadata overlay where necessary. This gives existing Molecule-based scripts a practical path into Registry discovery and client integration without requiring them to abandon Molecule or migrate their encoded data.

By establishing this lifecycle early—before script interfaces become fragmented across incompatible conventions—CKB can gain a shared interface layer that is language-neutral, verifiable, friendly to wallet builders, and open for ecosystem adoption.

While learning CKB, I studied the implications of its Cell Model and identified the lack of a standard, discoverable, machine-readable interface layer for scripts.

Current Status

The project has progressed beyond the idea stage. The core of the CKB IDL lifecycle has been designed and prototyped across several open-source repositories.

Completed or substantially implemented work includes:

  • IDL 0.1.0 specification: a dedicated specification repository defining the document structure, linear encoding profile, canonical JSON requirements, commitment model, error categories, conformance vectors, and compatibility guidance.

  • Rust derive and export tooling: ckb-idl-derive provides Rust macros for describing witness interfaces, including primitive types, fixed byte arrays, vectors, optional fields, nested structures, and explicitly tagged unions. A host-side exporter supports complete nested IDL generation.

  • Rust client library: ckb-idl-client can parse IDL documents, verify canonical commitments against a deployed executable’s binding trailer, validate witness bytes, and expose decoded witness data as structured objects.

  • Binding CLI: ckb-idl-cli provides commands for validating IDLs, generating and inspecting bindings, packaging artifacts, and verifying bound executables.

  • Reference lock scripts: multiple example lock scripts demonstrate optional fields, nested structures, tagged authorization choices, typed vectors, threshold/multisignature-style data, and commitment-based deployment artifacts.

  • Initial TypeScript work: an earlier TypeScript implementation exists and provides a starting point for the IDL 0.1.0 upgrade.

  • Community discussion: the initial interface-language proposal was published on Nervos Talk and introduced the derive, validate, and commitment direction to the ecosystem.

The work is now at the transition point from protocol/tooling prototypes to ecosystem infrastructure. The remaining work is to stabilize the released workflow, add Molecule compatibility, complete TypeScript support, and build the public registry through which scripts and their interfaces can be published, discovered, independently verified, and integrated.

Architecture & Design

The proposed system completes the CKB IDL lifecycle: script authors describe an interface, bind it to a deployable executable, publish it for discovery, and allow wallets or transaction builders to verify and consume it.

The full System Design Document is available here: CKB IDL System Design Document. It covers the data model, trust model, storage, deployment operations, security controls, and open design decisions in greater detail.

IDL 0.1.1 will add explicit support for empty witness interfaces. A script that requires no structured witness_args.lock payload still benefits from a discoverable identity, deployment record, verification status, documentation, and a machine-readable declaration that its lock-witness interface is intentionally empty.

Authoring and binding

Script authors define their witness interfaces through one of three paths:

  • Rust derives and exporter: Rust scripts use ckb-idl-derive to describe supported witness types and generate an IDL document.

  • Molecule-to-IDL generation: Molecule schemas are converted into compatible IDL documents, allowing existing Molecule-based scripts to join the same discovery and client workflow.

  • Manual legacy-IDL authoring: existing scripts without an embedded commitment can still publish a manually attested interface document.

The ckb-idl-cli validates the resulting IDL, canonicalizes it according to the IDL specification, calculates its SHA-256 digest, and appends a compact binding trailer to the compiled executable. The bound executable is then deployed as CKB code-cell data.

The trailer commits the deployed executable to the exact canonical IDL document. This gives a consumer a way to verify that an interface retrieved from the Registry actually corresponds to the deployed script.

Script Registry

The CKB Script Registry is an open-source, testnet-first discovery and evidence service for CKB scripts, independent of their implementation language, serialization format, or adoption of CKB IDL.

Scripts can be registered with or without an IDL document. Each registry entry can contain script identity, deployment references, publisher information, release metadata, source references, documentation, and optional interface artifacts.

CKB IDL is the first deeply supported interface standard, enabling cryptographically verifiable interface discovery and structured witness integration. Scripts without IDL remain discoverable, although they do not receive IDL-specific verification or encoding capabilities.

Scope and Focus

Although the Registry is designed as general-purpose infrastructure for CKB scripts, the primary focus of this proposal is completing the CKB IDL lifecycle. The Registry will accommodate scripts without IDL artifacts from its first release, ensuring that its architecture does not depend on adoption of a particular interface standard. However, the development effort, verification tooling, client integrations, and reference workflows funded by this grant will prioritize CKB IDL publication, discovery, verification, and consumption. Broader script-related capabilities can be developed incrementally without requiring a redesign of the Registry.

The initial registry architecture consists of:

  • a Rust API service for public reads, publisher authentication, package publication, validation, and release metadata

  • a background worker for CKB RPC verification, confirmation checks, code-cell liveness checks, retries, and candidate discovery

  • PostgreSQL for publishers, namespaces, releases, deployments, verification claims, jobs, and audit events;

  • content-addressed object storage for immutable IDL documents, manifests, and artifacts;

  • a TypeScript web frontend for search, package pages, interface inspection, deployment evidence, and integration guidance.

GitHub OAuth is sufficient for initial publisher authentication. CKB wallet ownership proofs will be added later, but are not necessary to establish the first useful publication workflow.

The registry is not a general-purpose transaction explorer. It focuses on script interfaces, artifacts, deployment evidence, and integration information, not generic chain analytics.

Consumer Verification

Wallets, SDKs, frontends, and transaction builders use the Registry for script discovery and integration information, but do not need to trust its claims blindly.

A consumer flow is:

  1. Resolve a script or package through the Registry.

  2. Retrieve its registered metadata, available artifacts, and deployment references.

  3. Independently verify the relevant deployment claims against CKB, including the referenced code cell and executable identity.

  4. Inspect the available interface artifacts, if any.

For scripts with a cryptographically bound CKB IDL:

  1. Retrieve the canonical IDL document and the deployed executable’s code-cell data.

  2. Read and validate the executable’s binding trailer.

  3. Canonicalize the retrieved IDL and calculate its SHA-256 digest.

  4. Confirm that the digest matches the commitment in the binding trailer.

  5. Use the verified interface to decode existing witness data or encode structured witness inputs for transaction construction.

For scripts with manually attested CKB IDLs:

  1. Retrieve the published IDL and its associated publisher attestation.

  2. Validate the IDL document against the specification and inspect its declared relationship to the script.

  3. Use the interface for encoding, decoding, or integration where appropriate, while recognizing that its correspondence to the executable has not been cryptographically established.

For scripts without CKB IDL:

  1. Access the available deployment information, source references, documentation, and integration guidance.

  2. Integrate using the script’s existing conventions or supported tooling.

These workflows distinguish verification of on-chain deployment facts from verification of interface commitments. A script may have independently verified deployment information without having a cryptographically bound IDL.

The Registry provides discovery and evidence rather than serving as a trusted authority. For bound interfaces, consumers can independently verify the IDL-to-executable relationship. For manually attested interfaces, the Registry identifies the source and limitations of the attestation without presenting it as equivalent to cryptographic binding.

Verification States

The registry records independent claims rather than presenting every listing as “verified”. A package may be:

  • Cryptographically bound: the canonical IDL digest matches the binding trailer in a deployed executable.

  • Manually attested: an identified publisher has documented an existing script without a trailer binding.

  • Unverified: submitted or discovered, but not yet sufficiently validated

  • Historical, spent, deprecated, or withdrawn: retained for transparency, but not presented as an active recommended deployment.

This allows existing scripts to be documented now without representing them as equivalent to newly bound IDL-enabled scripts.

Design rationale

The design is deliberately lightweight for the first release. It avoids arbitrary source builds, uploaded-code execution, on-chain Registry contracts, package dependency resolution, and a general explorer infrastructure. The Registry validates artifacts and chain facts; it does not execute scripts or claim to audit them.

This keeps the MVP focused on the core value proposition:

author → generate → validate → bind → deploy → publish → discover → verify → consume

It also provides a practical adoption path for both new Rust-based scripts and existing Molecule-based CKB development. The architecture is testnet-first, open-source, and designed to grow into mainnet support only after the publication, verification, resource-limit, and operational workflows have been demonstrated in practice.

Practical Use Cases, Ecosystem Integrations & Key Benefits for CKB

CKB IDL would provide a common interface layer for CKB scripts: one that makes script requirements understandable to both humans and software without weakening CKB’s flexibility or requiring a centralized authority to be trusted.

1. CCC: Generic Transaction Construction for Custom Scripts

CCC provides TypeScript transaction construction and wallet integration for CKB applications. Integrating an unfamiliar custom script still requires developers to understand its deployment, witness encoding, and transaction requirements.

CKB IDL would let CCC-based applications discover and verify published script interfaces, generate structured witness inputs, and encode witness data before passing transactions to CCC for signing and submission. This reduces script-specific integration work without replacing CCC’s existing responsibilities.

2. CellScript: Cross-Language Script Interoperability

CellScript already provides compiler-level interfaces, generated builders, and a registry for its development ecosystem. CKB IDL would complement these capabilities by providing a language-neutral interface artifact for deployed scripts.

CellScript-generated scripts could publish standard IDLs that Rust applications, TypeScript frontends, wallets, and other consumers can independently verify and use without understanding CellScript-specific compiler metadata.

3. Type Scripts: Programmable Game-State Transitions (Future)

A CKB game could represent player positions and game state using cells governed by Type Scripts. A future Type Script IDL profile could describe state-cell data, required move inputs, and structural transaction requirements, enabling frontends to construct transactions while the Type Script enforces valid state transitions.

This use case is outside the proposed IDL 0.1.1 scope but illustrates the value of extending CKB IDL beyond lock-witness interfaces.

4. A verifiable public registry

The Script Registry will provide a public place to search scripts, inspect interfaces, view deployment evidence, and find integration guidance. Importantly, it will not ask wallets to trust a registry database blindly. The registry is a discovery and evidence layer; the client can independently verify the IDL commitment embedded in the executable’s code-cell data.

This distinction is important for CKB: public convenience does not need to compromise self-verification.

Even when a script has no CKB IDL, developers can discover its registered identity, deployment locations, source references, and available documentation through the same Registry.

5. Support for existing as well as new scripts

Not every existing CKB script can be rebuilt with an IDL commitment. The Registry will support manually authored legacy IDLs, but label them distinctly from cryptographically bound interfaces. This allows the ecosystem to document important existing scripts immediately while preserving an honest trust model.

Out-of-Scope / Possible Future Funding Needs

This proposal is deliberately focused on a testnet-first, open-source implementation of the CKB IDL lifecycle and Script Registry. The following are not included in the requested $5,000 budget and may require later community discussion, follow-up grants, or independent funding.

  • Mainnet Registry launch and production SLA: Mainnet support will be considered only after testnet verification, backup recovery, monitoring, rate-limit testing, and client integration have been demonstrated.

  • Formal third-party security audit: The Registry does not execute uploaded code and this proposal does not deploy a new on-chain Registry contract. However, formal audits may be appropriate before a mainnet launch or if future on-chain components are introduced.

  • Long-term maintenance and infrastructure costs: The proposal covers development and initial testnet operation, not indefinite hosting, monitoring, support, or maintenance.

  • CKB wallet ownership proofs: MVP publisher authentication uses GitHub OAuth. Linking a publisher identity to CKB address ownership is a future enhancement.

  • Reproducible source-build verification: The Registry may link source code, but independently rebuilding source and proving it produces the registered executable requires controlled build infrastructure and is not included.

  • Type Script interface support: The initial IDL profile focuses on lock-witness interfaces. Type Script support requires separate design work, particularly around script arguments and hash_type = type resolution.

  • On-chain Registry contract, governance, or tokenomics: The first Registry is an off-chain discovery and evidence service. No Registry token, governance mechanism, or on-chain publication contract is proposed.

  • Full OpenZeppelin-style curated library or template marketplace: The Registry may later support recommendations and reusable templates, but the MVP focuses on verifiable artifact publication and discovery.

  • Full package dependency resolution: Package dependencies, version solving, and cross-package compatibility analysis are not required for the initial Registry.

  • Universal language and encoding support: Molecule integration and TypeScript support are included. Broader language bindings and support for other possible encoding systems are future work.

  • Multi-region high-availability infrastructure: The MVP does not include Kubernetes, multi-region active-active deployment, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Redis, or comparable operational complexity.

Risk & Mitigation

Risk Impact Mitigation
Registry scope becomes too broad Delays delivery or produces an incomplete product The project is limited to testnet, a focused publication/verification workflow, a basic public frontend, Molecule support for the supported profile, and TypeScript compatibility. Mainnet, audits, and marketplace features are explicitly deferred.
CKB deployment verification is more complex than expected May delay reliable verification of deployments or liveness. The Registry begins with reference scripts and a narrow binding-trailer verification path. Chain checks run in retryable background jobs and record explicit pending or failed states.
RPC outages, stale results, or reorganizations Deployment state may be temporarily uncertain. Store block evidence, use configurable confirmation thresholds, recheck liveness, use retries with backoff, and treat RPC failure as pending verification rather than failure.
Molecule mapping has unsupported constructs Some Molecule schemas may not map losslessly to IDL 0.1.0. Begin with a documented supported subset, publish clear errors for unsupported constructs, and validate against real schemas rather than promising universal coverage.
Low early Registry adoption Fewer publishers and interfaces at launch. Publish reference scripts, support manual legacy-IDL attestation, provide clear integration examples, and make the Registry useful even before broad ecosystem participation.
Misleading or malicious publisher metadata Users could mistake a listing for an audit or endorsement. Separate cryptographic binding, publisher identity, source availability, audit, and recommendation claims. Avoid a single generic “verified” badge
Resource-exhaustion or storage abuse Could increase cost or affect availability. Enforce upload, decompression, document-size, nesting-depth, queue, rate, and per-publisher limits. Use immutable blobs and cacheable public reads.
Solo-developer execution risk Delivery speed depends on one maintainer. Work is divided into independently demonstrable milestones, builds on already released tooling, uses open repositories, and keeps major future features out of scope.
CKB price volatility The CKB-denominated amount may fluctuate. The grant is requested as a USD equivalent, with each CKB disbursement calculated at the USD value at the time of payment.

Closing / Call to Action

CKB already enables developers to build highly flexible scripts. The missing layer is a shared, verifiable way for those scripts to describe their interfaces and for other developers to discover and safely integrate them, without needing to have pre-existing knowledge of the source code of the scripts.

The IDL 0.1.0 toolchain provides the foundation. This proposal funds the next step: a practical testnet lifecycle where interfaces can be generated from Rust or Molecule, bound to executables, published through an open Registry, independently verified by clients, and consumed by wallets and transaction builders.

The goal is not to create another centralized source of truth. It is to make CKB scripts easier to discover and reuse while preserving the ability of clients to verify the interface-to-executable relationship directly from CKB code-cell data.

Feedback on the Registry data model, Molecule integration, TypeScript workflow, verification policy, and testnet rollout is welcome. We appreciate the community’s consideration and look forward to building this openly with the CKB ecosystem.

Glossary

Term Meaning
Artifact An immutable published file or byte sequence, such as an IDL document, manifest, executable, or source archive.
Binding Trailer 1 The append-only metadata trailer, placed at the end of bound executable code-cell data. It contains the committed canonical IDL digest and metadata needed to parse it.
Bound executable A compiled script executable with a valid IDL binding trailer appended to its bytes.
Canonical IDL bytes Converting an IDL JSON document into one deterministic byte representation before hashing.
Canonicalization Converting an IDL JSON document into one deterministic byte representation before hashing.
CKB code cell A CKB cell whose data contains a script executable that can be referenced by a lock or type script.
Code hash The CKB hash used to identify executable code-cell data for script resolution.
Code-cell data hash A hash of the complete data stored in a specific code cell, including an IDL binding trailer where present.
Consumer A wallet, SDK, transaction builder, frontend, or other application that retrieves and uses an IDL.
Cryptographically bound An interface status indicating that the SHA-256 digest of canonical IDL bytes matches the digest stored in the deployed executable’s binding trailer.
Deployment A concrete on-chain location for an artifact, identified by network, transaction hash, and output index.
Deployment inclusion Evidence that a declared transaction output exists in an observed confirmed CKB block.
Deployment liveness The currently observed state of whether a code cell remains unspent and available on-chain.
Digest A fixed-length cryptographic hash output. IDL 0.1.0 uses SHA-256 for the canonical IDL commitment.
Encoding profile The rules used to serialize and deserialize fields in an IDL interface, such as the initial CKB IDL linear encoding profile.
Field path A stable path describing where a validation or decoding error occurred within an IDL document or witness object.
GitHub OAuth The initial publisher-authentication method used by the Registry. It verifies control of a GitHub account, not ownership of a CKB address.
Hash type The CKB script field that determines how code_hash should be interpreted, such as data or type.
IDL Interface Description Language: a machine-readable document describing a CKB script interface, its fields, types, encoding, and optional semantic labels.
IDL digest The SHA-256 hash of canonical IDL bytes. This is the value committed in Binding Trailer 1.
Legacy IDL A manually authored IDL for a script that does not contain an embedded binding trailer.
Manually attested An interface status indicating that a publisher supplied an IDL for a script but no cryptographic executable binding has been verified.
Manifest An immutable metadata document describing a publication bundle and its artifact digests.
Molecule A serialization framework widely used in the CKB ecosystem. The proposed Molecule integration generates compatible IDL documents from supported schemas.
Namespace A publisher-controlled naming scope used in package coordinates, such as publisher-name/package-name.
Object storage Blob storage used for immutable files such as IDLs, manifests, and optionally executables.
Outpoint A CKB reference to a specific transaction output, consisting of a transaction hash and output index.
Package A human-readable Registry project identity that may contain multiple immutable releases.
Publisher An authenticated account or organization that submits and manages Registry packages and releases.
Registry The off-chain discovery, publication, storage, and verification-evidence service for CKB script, their deployments, metadata, and optional interface artifacts.
Release An immutable versioned publication under a package coordinate, such as namespace/package@1.0.0.
Reorganization (reorg) A chain event in which previously observed blocks are replaced, requiring deployment evidence and confirmation status to be rechecked.
Semantic type An optional label that gives a structural field a wallet-facing meaning, such as an address, signature, public key, or amount.
Structural type / wire type The actual encoded representation of a field, such as u64, bytes, a fixed byte array, vector, struct, or union.
Testnet-first The rollout policy in which the first public Registry and verification workflow target CKB testnet before any mainnet deployment.
Transaction builder Software that assembles CKB transactions, including script arguments, witnesses, inputs, outputs, and signing data.
TypeScript client The planned frontend-oriented IDL library used to retrieve, verify, encode, and decode IDL interfaces in TypeScript applications.
Unverified A Registry state where an artifact or interface has been submitted or discovered but does not yet meet a defined verification status.
Witness object The structured in-memory representation of decoded witness fields that a client can validate, display, or encode into witness_args.lock.
Witness interface The IDL description of data expected in a script witness; IDL 0.1.0 initially focuses on witness_args.lock.

This is a much-needed piece of infrastructure for the CKB ecosystem.
One of the biggest barriers to building reusable applications on programmable blockchains is the amount of script-specific knowledge developers need before they can integrate with existing contracts or scripts. A standard, verifiable interface combined with a public registry could significantly reduce that friction for wallets, SDKs, transaction builders, and application developers.
I particularly like the distinction between cryptographically bound, manually attested, and unverified interfaces. Discoverability is useful, but discoverability with independently verifiable integrity is much more valuable.
One area I think deserves particular attention is the developer experience around adoption. The easier it is to generate IDLs from existing scripts, consume them through TypeScript tooling, and integrate discovery into existing development workflows, the more likely this becomes shared ecosystem infrastructure rather than another tool developers have to remember to use.
I’m also interested in how this could eventually extend beyond lock-witness interfaces to Type Scripts and more complex transaction-level requirements.
The bigger question for me is: how do we make CKB script interfaces discoverable and composable by default, so developers can build on existing scripts without needing to understand their internals or rely on centralized registries? If IDL can become a common standard across the ecosystem, it could be a significant step toward making CKB a genuinely composable smart contract platform.

I particularly like the distinction between cryptographically bound, manually attested, and unverified interfaces. Discoverability is useful, but discoverability with independently verifiable integrity is much more valuable.

One area I think deserves particular attention is the developer experience around adoption. The easier it is to generate IDLs from existing scripts, consume them through TypeScript tooling, and integrate discovery into existing development workflows, the more likely this becomes shared ecosystem infrastructure rather than another tool developers have to remember to use.

I’m also interested in how this could eventually extend beyond lock-witness interfaces to Type Scripts and more complex transaction-level requirements.

The bigger question for me is: how do we make CKB script interfaces discoverable and composable by default, so developers can build on existing scripts without needing to understand their internals or rely on centralized registries? If IDL can become a common standard across the ecosystem, it could be a significant step toward making CKB a genuinely composable smart contract platform.

topics.title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury

recent_posts.topic_title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
A small update on QuotaCell since I introduced it here last week.
I’ve now tested the shared spending allowance using signed transactions sent to an isolated CKB node, rather than relying only on the earlier contract tests.
For the test, Alice and Ben had separate keys and spending limits, but shared an overall allowance of 100 tokens.
Alice paid 60 successfully. Ben then tried to pay 50, but CKB rejected the transaction because only 40 remained in their shared allowance. When Ben tried 40 instead, it went through.
The final result was 100 spent between them, with another 100 tokens still protected in the treasury.
What I wanted to confirm was that the limit is enforced by CKB itself, not just by the application building the transactions. The owner didn’t need to approve each payment either.
I’ve also made the implementation, tests and transaction evidence public here:
github.com
GitHub - Ticoworld/QuotaCell: Experimental native CKB policy for shared...
Experimental native CKB policy for shared delegated spending, with verifier and isolated-node evidence.
This is still experimental work using synthetic tokens on a local development chain. There are important things left to handle, particularly payments happening at the same time, CKB capacity costs and making recovery easier for owners.
The earlier tests also cover permission changes and owner recovery, although those actions haven’t yet been demonstrated in the running-node test.
I appreciate the technical questions raised on the first post, especially around handling concurrent payments. They’ve helped clarify what still needs work.

topics.title: FiberNuts Community Market: A Testnet App for Cashu + Fiber

recent_posts.topic_title: FiberNuts Community Market: A Testnet App for Cashu + Fiber
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi, I tried market.fibernuts.xyz last night with two browser profiles, one as
attendee and one as vendor. Worked first time. The claim took about 1.5 s and a
coffee about 2 s until the vendor had fresh proofs. Nice work.
Some things I ran into:
I got the last faucet claim of the day (remainingToday went to 0 after 5).
With the per-network cap at 3 by default, an event on shared Wi-Fi would run
dry fast. Maybe an event code?
Once the faucet is empty, the only way in is paying a RUSD Fiber invoice, and
cashing out needs an invoice from another node. Most people at a stall won’t
have either.
The proofs are only in localStorage and I couldn’t find a backup step, so
clearing site data or Safari’s 7-day storage limit would lose the balance. Fine
for a demo, but a NUT-13 seed would help later.
No way back for the payer if a vendor never redeems. A NUT-11 locktime with the
payer as refund key would cover it, but payment.ts rejects those tags for now.
No CSP in market/vercel.json. With bearer proofs in localStorage it seems
worth adding.
Small ones: the cash screen says “1 claims left today”, and SECURITY.md says to
email but doesn’t give an address.

topics.title: Omiga v1.2.0 Release: Enhanced On-Chain Asset Management and Deeper CCC Integration

recent_posts.topic_title: Omiga v1.2.0 Release: Enhanced On-Chain Asset Management and Deeper CCC Integration
recent_posts.author: Oliver
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @phroi, thank you for the detailed write-up, and for taking the time to post it here even without an issue tracker to file it in.
You’re right: Omiga currently only tracks the Recommended CKB address of the connected wallet, so assets held under other locks that CCC derives from the same key aren’t surfaced. This is especially relevant for users coming over from Mobit, and we’ve taken note of it.
We’re now working on a plan to support moving assets from those older addresses to the new address smoothly, so that users don’t have to piece it together by hand. We expect to roll this out soon, and we’ll share an update in this thread once it’s available.
Thanks again for the feedback, and for the kind words on the CCC connector move!

topics.title: [DIS] Kaze X CKB Unitour Continuation Proposal

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Kaze X CKB Unitour Continuation Proposal
recent_posts.author: zz_tovarishch
recent_posts.content_text:
Based on the Metaforo tally at close, the outcome is PASSED. Approval is 100%, with total voting weight of 183,340,273 CKB from 13 voters. Both the approval threshold and minimum participation requirement are met.
Post-close verification was completed on 23 October 2026 using CKB DAO Watchdog, together with a manual sanity check. The verification cross-checks Metaforo-recorded voting weights against on-chain Nervos DAO deposit weights. In this run, 12 of 13 voters’ totals match exactly.
One Yes entry is flagged because the voter’s current on-chain deposits are 300,000 CKB higher than the weight Metaforo recorded. The difference comes from a single new deposit made after the vote was cast—the same deposit reviewed during the RIVET verification. The deposits held at the time of voting match the recorded 10,194,000 CKB exactly, and all remain unspent in the DAO. The additional deposit was not included in the recorded vote weight, so there was no vote inflation. Including it would increase total voting weight to 183,640,273 CKB, while approval would remain 100%.
No voter appears under both options, and no bound address appears under more than one voting account in the verification records.
These checks support the PASSED result for the Kaze × CKB UniTour Continuation Proposal.
